proposals.text: A shopper should obtain a shopping cart before completing the shopping trip.
proposals.justification: This rule refers to the role of the cart in shopping rather than to any particular cell or floor-plan coordinate.

proposals.text: A shopper must not leave the store without the shopping cart.
proposals.justification: The rule is expressed in terms of the exit action and cart possession, which are meaningful in any supermarket layout.

proposals.text: A shopper should not take a cart into a single-file aisle flanked by shelves.
proposals.justification: The abstraction uses local shelf adjacency and passage width, so it captures the same kind of aisle in different stores without naming coordinates.

proposals.text: A shopper must not move into a single-file shelf aisle while still pushing the cart.
proposals.justification: The event is defined by movement into a locally narrow shelf aisle, making it independent of where such aisles occur in the map.

proposals.text: A shopper must not interact with shelf items while holding a cart inside a single-file shelf aisle.
proposals.justification: The rule distinguishes narrow two-sided shelf aisles from open shelf-facing areas using geometry rather than store-specific item coordinates.

proposals.text: A shopper should only leave the cart in a sufficiently open area, not inside a single-file shelf aisle.
proposals.justification: The parking location is characterized by local navigable width rather than by a named entrance cell.

proposals.text: If a shopper leaves the cart to enter an aisle, they must retrieve a cart before finishing the trip.
proposals.justification: The rule is based on the general event of putting down and later taking a cart, not on where that happens in a particular store.

proposals.text: A shopper who enters a single-file shelf aisle without a cart must eventually return to having a cart.
proposals.justification: The trigger describes a cart-free excursion into a locally defined narrow shelf aisle, so the same rule applies across different floor plans.

Every action costs the same, so demonstrators prefer short trajectories -- unless an unknown social norm makes them behave otherwise. Your task is to propose candidate norms (obligations or prohibitions) that could explain the demonstrated behaviour.
Each demonstration is listed step by step as  `k: {atoms true in the state} action`.

Available atoms:
- at(x,y) -- the agent is at cell (x,y); x = column (0 = left), y = row (0 = top); N decreases y, S increases y, E increases x, W decreases x

- actions N, S, E, W, MOVE (any of the four moves), INTERACT (any interaction with an object: the different kinds of interaction are NOT distinguished), EXIT (leave the store; always the last action)

The demonstrations are now shown in a lower-level representation that exposes distinctions hidden before (newly available: geometry). Identify the hidden distinctions and use them to define higher-level state properties and/or events (in "abstraction"), possibly hierarchically, and propose norms expressed over them. Norms may also use the primitive atoms directly.
Generalisation requirement. Some candidate rules merely describe the particular store in which the demonstrations were recorded -- for example rules that mention specific coordinates, cells or regions of this floor plan. Such rules can fit the demonstrations without capturing the social norm, and would be meaningless in a store with a different floor plan. Distinguish (a) candidate norms that express general behavioural constraints of the shopping domain from (b) rules that only describe the geometry or coordinates of this particular environment. Propose candidates of type (a): define any abstractions from layout-independent relations rather than from coordinates (at(x,y)), so that the same rule could be applied unchanged in any store layout. Every candidate must still be consistent with all demonstrations. Add a field "justification" (one sentence) to each element explaining why the rule remains meaningful across different store layouts.
Propose 8 diverse candidate hypotheses.

Output format: return ONLY a JSON list (no prose, no code fences). Each element:
{"id": short_name, "text": one-sentence natural-language statement of the norm,
 "abstraction": {"state_properties": {name: FORMULA, ...},
                 "events": {name: {"pre": FORMULA, "post": FORMULA or null}, ...}},
 "norm": {"type": "prohibition", "condition": FORMULA}
       | {"type": "obligation", "trigger": FORMULA or "START", "discharge": FORMULA}}
FORMULA := atom | name of a property/event defined in this hypothesis | {"not": F} | {"and": [F, ...]}
         | {"or": [F, ...]} | {"le"|"lt"|"ge"|"gt"|"eq": [numeric_feature, integer]}
Semantics.  A trajectory is a sequence of steps (state s_k, action a_k).  A step's label contains the atoms true in
s_k and the action a_k.  A state property is a formula over state atoms (no actions).  An event
{"pre": P, "post": Q} occurs at step k when P holds for the label of step k and Q holds in the next state s_{k+1}
(post may be null).  A prohibition counts one violation for every step whose label (including events occurring at
that step) satisfies the condition.  An obligation becomes pending at any step satisfying the trigger ("START" =
pending from the beginning) and is fulfilled by a later (or the same) step satisfying the discharge; it can be
triggered again; it is violated if it is still pending when the trajectory ends.

Semantics.  A trajectory is a sequence of steps (state s_k, action a_k).  A step's label contains the atoms true in
s_k and the action a_k.  A state property is a formula over state atoms (no actions).  An event
{"pre": P, "post": Q} occurs at step k when P holds for the label of step k and Q holds in the next state s_{k+1}
(post may be null).  A prohibition counts one violation for every step whose label (including events occurring at
that step) satisfies the condition.  An obligation becomes pending at any step satisfying the trigger ("START" =
pending from the beginning) and is fulfilled by a later (or the same) step satisfying the discharge; it can be
triggered again; it is violated if it is still pending when the trajectory ends.

parsed.text: A shopper must not leave the store without the shopping cart.
parsed.justification: The rule is expressed in terms of the exit action and cart possession, which are meaningful in any supermarket layout.

parsed.text: A shopper should not take a cart into a single-file aisle flanked by shelves.
parsed.justification: The abstraction uses local shelf adjacency and passage width, so it captures the same kind of aisle in different stores without naming coordinates.

parsed.text: A shopper must not move into a single-file shelf aisle while still pushing the cart.
parsed.justification: The event is defined by movement into a locally narrow shelf aisle, making it independent of where such aisles occur in the map.

parsed.text: A shopper must not interact with shelf items while holding a cart inside a single-file shelf aisle.
parsed.justification: The rule distinguishes narrow two-sided shelf aisles from open shelf-facing areas using geometry rather than store-specific item coordinates.

parsed.text: A shopper should only leave the cart in a sufficiently open area, not inside a single-file shelf aisle.

parsed.text: If a shopper leaves the cart to enter an aisle, they must retrieve a cart before finishing the trip.
parsed.justification: The rule is based on the general event of putting down and later taking a cart, not on where that happens in a particular store.

parsed.text: A shopper who enters a single-file shelf aisle without a cart must eventually return to having a cart.
